html:
The Inca Empire, Tawantinsuyu or "the four parts together", was the largest state of the Americas before Europeans came. From its capital at Cusco it ruled along the Andes from Ecuador to central Chile between 1438 and 1533.

Its growth was fast. The Inca had been one small kingdom among many until Pachacuti won a war against the Chanka, conventionally in 1438. He, his son Topa Inca Yupanqui and his grandson Huayna Capac conquered in under a century lands home to perhaps ten million people, including the coastal kingdom of Chimor.

The empire worked without markets, money, the wheel, iron or writing. It ran on:

  • Labour service, called mit'a: households owed work to the state, on farms, roads, mines or in the army.
  • Roads: the Inca road system, about 40,000 km long, with runners carrying messages.
  • Storehouses full of food and cloth (see Inca storehouses).
  • Records kept on the knotted cords of the quipu.
  • Resettlement: whole communities were moved to secure new lands.
  • Quechua, spread as the common language.

Huayna Capac died around 1527, probably of smallpox, which had arrived ahead of the Spanish. His sons Huáscar and Atahualpa then fought a civil war. Atahualpa had just won when Francisco Pizarro seized him at Cajamarca in 1532 (see Atahualpa captured). The Spanish took Cusco in 1533. A Neo-Inca state held out at Vilcabamba until 1572, and Quechua is still spoken by millions in the Andes.
